content: Pyrazinamide should always be administered in combination with other effective antituberculous drugs. It is typically used during the initial two months of a six-month or longer treatment regimen for patients with drug-susceptible tuberculosis. For patients who are known or suspected to have drug-resistant tuberculosis, treatment regimens should be tailored to their specific clinical situation. Pyrazinamide often plays a critical role in such individualized therapies. Patients with concurrent HIV infection may require extended courses of therapy. Physicians managing these patients should remain vigilant for any updated recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) regarding this specific population. The usual dose of pyrazinamide is administered orally at 15 to 30 mg/kg once daily. While older regimens involved dividing the daily dose into three or four smaller doses, current guidelines recommend a single daily dose. The maximum daily dose should not exceed 3 grams. However, the CDC guidelines recommend a maximum of 2 grams per day when used as part of a daily regimen. An alternative twice-weekly dosing regimen has been developed to improve patient adherence, particularly in outpatient settings. This regimen involves administering 50 to 75 mg/kg of pyrazinamide twice weekly, based on lean body weight. In studies evaluating this twice-weekly regimen, doses exceeding 3 grams twice weekly have been used, which surpasses the recommended maximum daily dose of 3 grams. Despite this, no increased incidence of adverse reactions has been reported. These recommendations are derived from the joint guidelines issued by the CDC and the American Thoracic Society.
